title: Dapplefoot and the Purrfect Prize
markdown:
Faeloria tucked itself behind whispering peaks that looked like giant emerald stairs, and ordinary maps forgot it on purpose. Dapplefoot the ogre was not the grump-and-stomp sort. Softer than moss on an old tree, eyes kind as summer sky, fingers quick for carving birds that almost flew. His home in the mountainside was quiet as a brook that had learned manners. Patch, a puff of white with one black ear and eyes like little green jewels, was a whirlwind whose hobby was vanishing and whose talent was being found at the worst height.

The Annual Village Wonder Contest filled the square: rainbow silks, gourds with ambition, carvings that looked ready to hop, banners like birds. Dapplefoot was not looking at shine. Patch was gone again, sneakiest hiding spot in a career of sneaks. High, low, behind sunbeams, under mushroom hats. Then up: a tiny white tail on the Grand Prize—a tower of stones and wooden birds that belonged to Elder Hemlock, who loved it the way some people love their own hats.

“Scamp,” Dapplefoot rumbled, far thunder. Tricky.

Elf Nessa arrived, falling-snow quiet, bells for a voice. “Trouble?”

“The prize.”

“Lively magic in that pile. And—” she nodded at the market—“Whizbang and Willowyn are at it.”

Wizard Whizbang, silver beard, eyes huge behind glass, floated a teacup. Witch Willowyn, dark curls, mischief employed, set it spinning. Friendly duel, dazzling, a little contagious.

“No rush,” Dapplefoot said, large hands folded. “Tea first.” A stone, a striped blanket that appeared because he liked sitting done properly. Patch blinked from altitude.

“Judges,” Nessa reminded, fond.

Cups drifted; broomsticks jigged Whizbang’s nose. Villagers smiled with a crease of worry. “Feather duster for your beard!” “Self-stirring pot is hungry!”

Dapplefoot watched. Noise fed the magic. Patch yawned: the cup wobbled. Patch stretched: a wooden bird tried its wings. The kitten was conducting without applying.

“His purrs. Sleepy stretches. Soft nudges. A loud purr might settle it.”

“From up there?”

He drew a carved wooden mouse, Patch’s, and wiggled. A mew descended. Wiggle, more fun. Then the lullaby: warm milk, blankets, the particular hum of an ogre who meant nap. Patch’s head tilted. Comfort won. A rumble started, bigger than Dapplefoot’s sigh, happiness with a motor.

Teacups remembered gentleness. Brooms went home. Beard stilled. Square exhaled. Hemlock, hand off his chest, found his prize intact. “Well, I never.”

Dapplefoot stood, still humming, palm up, careful as a shelf. Patch leapt, landed, became a white comma on a warm chest.

He did not tell the village that quiet magic was the biggest kind. He scratched the black ear. Nessa’s bells rang once, private. The judges, when they came, judged gourds. Patch, employed as a paperweight against further wonders, purred the rest of the morning into place.
characters: Dapplefoot (ogre Dapplefoot), Patch (kitten Patch), Nessa (elf Nessa)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
author: StoryGen Community
